q: A 200 g orphaned kitten needs tube feeding. What is the maximum safe single-feeding volume, given neonatal stomach capacity?
o: 2 mL
9 mL
22 mL
40 mL
e: Stomach capacity is about 40 to 50 mL/kg; 0.2 kg x 45 mL/kg is roughly 9 mL. Exceeding it risks reflux and fatal aspiration.

q: A 10-day-old kitten is hypothermic (91 F / 32.8 C), hypoglycemic, and recumbent. What is the correct initial sequence?
o: Immediately tube-feed 10 mL of warm milk replacer
Rewarm to near-normothermia first, then give warm fluids with dextrose (SC or IO), withholding oral intake until normothermic
Give a cold SC dextrose bolus and a warm water bath
Inject enrofloxacin and place in a 105 F (40.6 C) incubator
e: A cold gut has ileus; feeding ferments milk and causes endotoxemia. Rewarm first, then warm dextrose-containing fluids; feed only once normothermic.

q: A litter of 4-week-old kittens is ready to wean. Which method is correct?
o: Abruptly remove the queen and offer dry adult kibble in a deep bowl
Offer a warm semisolid slurry of kitten food in a shallow pan, completing weaning from formula by 5 to 6 weeks
Bottle-feed formula exclusively until 8 weeks
Feed ground raw beef with cow's milk by syringe pump
e: Weaning starts at 3 to 4 weeks with a warm semisolid slurry in a shallow pan; complete weaning from formula by 5 to 6 weeks.

q: Cats in a ward cleaned with a quaternary ammonium disinfectant at 4x the correct dilution develop hypersalivation, anorexia, and tongue ulcers. What is the cause?
o: An immune reaction to DA2PP antigens
Caustic mucosal injury from grooming residual quaternary ammonium compound off the fur
Systemic organophosphate toxicity from run-off
Permethrin neurotoxicity of cranial nerves
e: Improperly diluted quaternary ammonium compounds are caustic; cats groom the residue off and develop glossal ulceration and hypersalivation.

q: Why are cats uniquely sensitive to permethrin?
o: No functional renal filtration of lipophilic compounds
A genetic deficiency of hepatic glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A6 is a pseudogene), impairing conjugation and prolonging exposure
High density of dermal nicotinic receptors
Structural fragility of feline hemoglobin
e: Cats have a UGT (glucuronidation) deficiency, not a complete absence; this contributes to permethrin sensitivity through accumulation of potent metabolites.

q: An 11-year-old arthritic dog at 5 months in the shelter is reactive, anorexic, and curled in the back corner 90% of the time. Which finding confirms an unlivable QOL state?
o: Greeting a familiar caretaker who brings high-value treats
Constant hyper-vigilance, inability to rest relaxed, and a persistent shift toward unpleasant over pleasant states
Occasional vocalization when neighboring dogs are moved
Stable body weight and BCS on monthly audits
e: QOL is the balance of feelings; persistent hyper-vigilance, no relaxed rest, and dominance of unpleasant states indicate an unlivable state.

q: How does McMillan's model define quality of life?
o: A checklist of normal vital signs
The animal's affective and cognitive assessment of its life as a balance of pleasant and unpleasant feelings
The number of enrichment items in the enclosure
The veterinarian's prognosis score
e: QOL is the animal's affective and cognitive self-assessment, driven by the balance of pleasant versus unpleasant feelings.

q: Which is a recognized stress indicator in shelter cats?
o: Increased exploratory play in the first 24 hours
Hiding, apathy, low activity, and feigned sleep, with hiding negatively correlated with cortisol
A rising body weight in week one
Eager approach to unfamiliar handlers
e: Hiding, apathy, low activity, and feigned sleep indicate feline stress; hiding negatively correlates with cortisol and aids coping.

q: Which set of signs indicates stress in a newly admitted shelter dog?
o: Relaxed posture and steady appetite
Displacement behaviors, looking back at the handler, lip licking, body shaking, and yawning
A single bark at intake then settling
Immediate solicitation of play
e: Displacement behaviors, lip licking, yawning, body shaking, and looking back at the handler are early canine stress signs.

q: On the Villalobos HHHHHMM (H5M2) scale, what cumulative score generally indicates that quality of life has become unacceptable?
o: Below 35 out of 70
Above 60 out of 70
Exactly 50 out of 70
Any score with mobility above 5
e: Each of the seven variables is scored 0 to 10; a total above 35 suggests acceptable QOL, and below 35 suggests it has become unacceptable.

q: What does the AAFCO statement of nutritional adequacy on a pet-food label indicate?
o: The product is organic and grain-free
How the diet meets nutritional requirements and for which life stage; it should not be expired
The wholesale price of the product
That the food was made in the United States
e: The AAFCO statement indicates nutritional adequacy and life stage; AAFCO sets pet-food standards, and the statement should not be expired.

q: Which nutrients must cats obtain pre-formed because they cannot synthesize them adequately?
o: Vitamin C and fiber
Taurine, arginine, and vitamin A
Calcium and phosphorus only
Omega-9 fatty acids and starch
e: As obligate carnivores, cats require pre-formed taurine, arginine, and vitamin A, which a meat-derived diet supplies.

q: What is the standard ceiling for treats as a fraction of an animal's daily caloric intake?
o: Up to 50%
No more than 10%
Between 25 and 40%
Unlimited if the diet is complete and balanced
e: The standard is the 10% rule: treats should not exceed 10% of daily calories (correcting the 10 to 25% figure in the dog notes).

q: Why are raw diets discouraged for shelter cats and dogs?
o: They are too expensive to source
They are seldom nutritionally balanced and carry bacterial contamination and public-health risk
They cause immediate vitamin A toxicity
They are banned by AAFCO in all states
e: Raw and home-cooked diets are seldom balanced and carry contamination and zoonotic risk (for example salmonella).

q: What is the difference between RER and MER?
o: RER is for cats and MER is for dogs
RER is baseline resting energy; MER applies a life-stage and activity factor to RER
They are identical terms
MER is only used for neonates
e: RER is the resting energy requirement; MER multiplies RER by a life-stage and activity factor for maintenance.

q: Why are large, deep-chested dogs fed twice daily or more often?
o: To increase their treat allowance
To help reduce the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV)
Because they cannot digest dry food
To speed weight gain for adoption photos
e: Splitting feeding across the day helps reduce GDV risk in large, deep-chested dogs.

q: Which feeding method is most appropriate for a group-housed room of healthy cats?
o: A single communal bowl of canned food refilled weekly
Free-choice dry food kept fresh and topped up, with monitoring since non-eaters can be missed
Withholding food except for one supervised meal per week
Raw meat left out at room temperature
e: Free-choice dry food suits group-housed cats (canned spoils), but monitor because animals not eating can go unnoticed.

q: An adult cat in the shelter has refused all food for 4 days. Why is prompt examination important?
o: Risk of immediate rabies shedding
Risk of hepatic lipidosis
It will void the cat's AAFCO warranty
It indicates the cat is pregnant
e: Adult cats not eating for 3 to 5 days risk hepatic lipidosis and need prompt examination.

q: When refeeding a chronically starved animal, what is the principal danger?
o: Immediate obesity
Refeeding syndrome from electrolyte shifts (phosphate, potassium, magnesium), causing weakness, seizures, and death
Permanent taurine depletion
Food aversion to all future diets
e: Rapid refeeding causes dangerous electrolyte shifts (refeeding syndrome); reintroduce nutrition gradually with monitoring.

q: How often must uneaten food be discarded in shelter feeding protocols?
o: Once per week
At least every 24 hours, and immediately if contaminated or pest-infested
Only when visibly moldy
Never, to reduce waste
e: Discard uneaten food at least every 24 hours, and immediately if contaminated or pest-infested.

q: What is the recommended feeding interval for neonates during the first few days of life?
o: Every 8 hours
Every 2 to 3 hours
Once daily
Free-choice dry food
e: Neonates are fed every 2 to 3 hours for the first few days, then every 4 to 5 hours until 3 weeks.

q: What environmental temperature is appropriate for orphaned neonates in the first week of life?
o: 85 to 95 F (29 to 35 C), dropping about 5 F (~2.8 C) per week
Room temperature is sufficient
e: First-week neonatal environmental temperature is about 85 to 95 F (29.4 to 35°C), dropping roughly 5 F (2.8°C) per week to 70 to 75 F (21.1 to 23.9°C) by week 4.

q: A litter shows fading kitten syndrome. Which is part of correct supportive care?
o: Feed the cold kittens immediately to correct energy deficit
Rewarm first, then provide tube feeding, SC fluids, and active warming, treat littermates, and rule out panleukopenia
Place all kittens in a freezer to slow metabolism
Give a single oral NSAID and observe
e: Rewarm before feeding, then supportive care (tube feeding, SC fluids, warming), treat littermates, and rule out FPV.

q: What is the approximate gestation length in the cat?
o: About 42 days
About 65 days
About 90 days
About 115 days
e: Feline gestation is about 65 days, typically producing 3 to 5 kittens.

q: By which day of feline pregnancy is serum relaxin typically elevated enough to support a diagnosis?
o: Day 5
Day 25
Day 50
Day 60
e: Serum relaxin is elevated by about day 25; ultrasound can detect pregnancy as early as day 10, and palpation from day 14 to 17.

q: Using dentition, a male cat with permanent canines but small testes is approximately what age?
o: 6 to 9 months
Under 8 weeks
18 to 24 months
Over 5 years
e: Permanent canines with small testes suggest about 6 to 9 months; mature testes suggest 12 to 14 months.

q: An orphan kitten weighs 100 g at birth. What daily weight gain should prompt concern?
o: A gain of 10 to 15 g per day
A gain under 7 g per day
Any gain at all
A gain over 5 g per day
e: Neonatal kittens should gain 10 to 15 g/day; under 7 g/day is inadequate and signals supplemental feeding or a health problem.

q: Why should kittens under 6 to 8 weeks of age generally not be housed in the shelter?
o: They cannot be microchipped at that age
High infection risk; foster care is strongly preferred
A legal hold requires it
They are too young to be photographed for adoption
e: Kittens under 6 to 8 weeks are at high infection risk and are best placed in foster care rather than housed in the shelter.

q: Feline acetaminophen toxicity (methemoglobinemia, Heinz-body anemia) is best explained by:
o: Glucuronidation deficiency alone
Both deficient glucuronidation (UGT1A6) and a lack of N-acetyltransferase 2, with the p-aminophenol pathway driving methemoglobinemia
A receptor mutation in erythrocytes
Excess hepatic glucuronidation
e: Feline acetaminophen toxicity is multifactorial: deficient UGT glucuronidation plus NAT2 deficiency, with p-aminophenol producing methemoglobinemia.

q: Which household or shelter item is a recognized feline toxicant to avoid?
o: Plain fresh water
Baby food containing onion powder, and lilies
A complete and balanced commercial cat diet
A clean stainless steel bowl
e: Onion (including onion-powder baby foods) causes hemolytic anemia and lilies are nephrotoxic; both must be avoided in cats.

q: The approximate daily water requirement for a healthy adult cat eating dry food is:
o: 5 mL/kg/day
50 mL/kg/day (approximately double what a wet-food cat needs)
200 mL/kg/day
Water requirements are the same regardless of diet type
e: Cats need approximately 50 mL/kg/day; dry-food cats must drink nearly twice as much as wet-food cats because wet food provides 70–80% water content.

q: A shelter cat on an exclusively dry diet develops recurrent urinary crystals. The most likely contributing nutritional factor is:
o: Excess dietary taurine
Insufficient voluntary water intake, producing chronically concentrated urine
Excessive wet-food supplementation
Overfeeding of treats
e: Dry-only diets increase urine concentration; cats have a low thirst drive relative to water needs, making urinary tract disease a real risk when only dry food is offered.

q: Signs of ≥ 5% dehydration on physical examination include:
o: Normal skin tent and moist mucous membranes
Skin tent persisting > 1–2 seconds, tacky or dry mucous membranes, and sunken eyes
Increased urination and drooling
Bounding pulse and hyperactivity
e: At ≥ 5% dehydration: persistent skin tent, tacky/dry mucous membranes, and sunken eyes. At ≥ 10%: depression, weak pulse, prolonged CRT.

q: The preferred water delivery method in a shelter with biosecurity concerns is:
o: Communal water troughs shared among multiple animals
Individual water bowls per animal or per enclosure, cleaned daily
Weekly water bucket changes
Standing pans refilled monthly
e: Community troughs are fomite transmission risks. Individual water bowls per enclosure, scrubbed and sanitized on the same schedule as food bowls, are the biosecurity-correct approach.

q: Per ASV guidance, raw meat diets are NOT recommended in shelter settings primarily because:
o: They are too expensive for non-profit organizations
They carry Salmonella and Campylobacter shedding risk to immunocompromised animals and staff, are seldom nutritionally balanced, and pose regulatory concerns in multi-animal facilities
They are incompatible with AAFCO labeling requirements
They cause taurine deficiency in cats
e: The ASV advises against raw diets in shelters due to zoonotic risk, nutritional imbalance, and regulatory concerns. Multiple Salmonella outbreaks have been linked to raw feeding in shelters.

q: Wet or canned food left in an open can at room temperature should be discarded after:
o: 72 hours
24 hours
2 hours
1 week
e: Opened wet food should be refrigerated and discarded after 2 hours at room temperature to prevent bacterial growth. Feral cat protocol extends this to 4–6 hours maximum under careful monitoring.

q: The safe target rate of weight loss in an obese shelter cat is:
o: 5–10% of body weight per week
1–2% of body weight per week
0.1% of body weight per week
As fast as possible to reduce length of stay
e: Safe weight loss is 1–2% of body weight per week. Faster loss in cats triggers peripheral fat mobilization faster than the liver can process, risking hepatic lipidosis.

q: An obese cat (BCS 8/9, 7 kg (15.4 lb)) has not eaten for 4 days in the shelter. The highest-priority concern is:
o: The cat needs more environmental enrichment
Hepatic lipidosis from fat mobilization into the liver during voluntary anorexia
The cat is on a successful self-imposed weight-loss fast
The BCS will normalize without intervention
e: Obese cats mobilizing peripheral fat rapidly when anorexic are at high risk of hepatic lipidosis. Veterinary exam and assisted feeding are indicated within 48–72 hours of anorexia.

q: The correct dietary approach for an obese cat (BCS 9/9) requiring weight loss is:
o: Abrupt caloric restriction to 50% of maintenance to produce rapid weight loss
Gradual reduction targeting 1–2% body weight loss per week, maintaining adequate protein, with veterinary oversight
Withholding all food for 3 days then resuming a normal diet
Switching immediately to a low-fat raw diet
e: Gradual restriction at 1–2%/week with protein maintenance prevents hepatic lipidosis. Rapid caloric reduction is dangerous in obese cats and can trigger the exact hepatic crisis the diet change is trying to prevent.

q: For a 30 kg (66.1 lb) obese dog, the target weekly weight loss at the safe 1–2% rate is approximately:
o: 3–6 kg (6.6–13.2 lb) per week
300–600 g per week
30–60 g per week
1–2 g per week
e: 1–2% of 30 kg (66.1 lb) = 300–600 g per week. This rate allows meaningful progress while avoiding the metabolic complications of crash dieting.

q: According to the 2026 ASV Guidelines for Humane Rabbit Housing, what is the 'rabbit comfort zone' temperature range?
e: The rabbit comfort zone is 59–72°F (15–22°C). Rabbits are very sensitive to heat stress above 86°F (30°C) and have limited thermoregulatory capacity in warm environments.

q: What is the minimum acceptable primary enclosure floor area for a single rabbit in a shelter, and for how long may this size be used?
o: 33 ft²/3 m²; no time limit
8–11 ft²/0.8–1 m²; less than 2 weeks only
5 ft²/0.5 m²; indefinitely if enrichment is provided
18 ft²/1.7 m²; up to 1 month
e: Minimum acceptable size is 8–11 ft²/0.8–1 m² and is a temporary measure only — does not include integrated exercise space and may only be used for stays under 2 weeks.

q: A rabbit has been housed in a minimum acceptable enclosure (0.9 m²) (9.7 sq ft) for 3 weeks awaiting surgery. What does this represent and what action is required?
o: No concern; the enclosure meets ASV minimum acceptable standards
Welfare compromise — the minimum acceptable enclosure may only be used for stays under 2 weeks; the rabbit must be moved to a larger enclosure, foster care, or an adoptive home
The enclosure is adequate as long as enrichment items are provided daily
The rabbit should be moved to a wire-floor surgical recovery cage for hygiene
e: Minimum acceptable enclosures are for stays under 2 weeks only. Rabbits housed longer develop musculoskeletal and GI problems, elevated corticosterone, and activity rebound — all welfare compromise indicators.

q: What is the minimum recommended primary enclosure size for a single rabbit on a long-term shelter stay, per ASV 2026?
o: 33 ft² / 3 m², length 9–10 ft/3 m, width ≥ 3 ft/0.9 m
45 ft² / 4 m² with width ≥ 5 ft/1.5 m
5 ft² / 0.5 m² with daily supplemental exercise
e: 33 ft²/3 m² with an unobstructed run of 3 m is the minimum recommended for long-stay single rabbits — includes integrated exercise space accessible at all times.

q: Why are motion-activated lighting systems specifically contraindicated in rabbit housing areas?
o: They produce excess heat that disrupts the rabbit comfort zone
Rabbits active at night trigger the system, disrupting the critical dark phase of their circadian rhythm
They emit UVB radiation harmful to rabbit retinas
They are too loud and exceed the 50 dB noise threshold
e: Motion-activated systems are triggered by rabbit activity at night, disrupting the dark phase of the light/dark cycle. Disruption causes reduced stress adaptation, altered immune function, and shortened lifespan.

q: What is the minimum ambient light intensity specified for rabbit housing by the ASV 2026 guideline?
o: 1 footcandle (10 lux)
3–5 footcandles (30–50 lux)
30–50 footcandles (300–500 lux)
0 footcandles; rabbits need full darkness at all times
e: Minimum resting light intensity is 3–5 FC (30–50 lux). Higher levels (30–50 FC) are needed only for observation and cleaning. Constant high-intensity light is stressful for rabbits.

q: Prolonged exposure to what decibel range is specifically identified as detrimental to rabbit hearing by the ASV 2026 guideline?
e: 50–70 dB — equivalent to normal conversation through vacuum cleaner level — is specifically detrimental to rabbit hearing. Shelters regularly exceed 100 dB; rabbit housing must be in the quietest area available.

q: A rabbit released from a minimum acceptable enclosure after 3 weeks launches across the room in explosive locomotor bursts. What does this behavior most likely represent?
o: Normal energetic play appropriate for the rabbit's age and breed
Activity rebound from behavioral deprivation in an undersized enclosure — a recognized welfare indicator
An emerging neurological disorder requiring a workup
Aggression directed at enrichment items
e: Activity rebound (explosive locomotion when given space) is a specific indicator of prior behavioral deprivation. It signals that the rabbit was housed below welfare standards and is a recognized welfare outcome measure in rabbit husbandry research.

q: Which flooring type is specifically contraindicated for rabbit primary enclosures per the ASV 2026 guideline?
o: Rubber matting
Slatted, grid, or wire flooring
Vinyl tile
Woven grass mats
e: Wire and slatted floors cause pododermatitis (sore hocks) from pressure and abrasion. Solid flooring covered with appropriate bedding is required. This is one of the most common housing welfare failures in rabbit care.

q: What are the four components of a complete rabbit primary enclosure per ASV 2026?
o: Sleeping area, food station, grooming area, and play tunnel
Hiding/resting space, elimination area (litter box), eating/drinking area, and exercise/play space
Feeding station, water source, UV light panel, and outdoor run
Nest box, squeeze panel, food puzzle, and climbing structure
e: The 4 required components are: (1) hiding/resting space, (2) elimination area/litter box, (3) eating/drinking area, (4) exercise/play space. All four must be present in the primary enclosure.

q: What is the recommended litter box configuration for shelter rabbits per ASV 2026?
o: Small corner litter box with clay litter, one shared per three rabbits
At least one large litter box per rabbit, placed in a corner or periphery, with hay accessible from inside the box; avoid small corner-style litter boxes even for small rabbits
A single large communal litter tray in the center of the enclosure
Newspaper sheets on the floor replacing traditional litter boxes
e: One large litter box per rabbit is required, placed in the corner or periphery, and hay must be accessible from inside the box. Corner litter boxes are specifically identified as too small even for small rabbits.

q: What water delivery method is preferred for rabbits per ASV 2026?
o: Water bottles, because they prevent contamination and drowning
Open water dishes, because rabbits prefer to drink from open water surfaces; water bottles are acceptable only under specific circumstances
Water provided only at mealtimes to monitor intake
Shared community water bowls changed twice weekly
e: Rabbits prefer to drink from open water surfaces. Open dishes are preferred; water bottles may be used under specific circumstances. For unknown intake rabbits, offer both until preference is established.

q: Why is acetic acid (vinegar) specifically useful in rabbit housing sanitation?
o: It is an effective disinfectant against RHDV
It dissolves alkaline mineral deposits from rabbit urine that standard alkaline soaps cannot remove
It neutralizes cecotroph odor
It is a topical antiseptic for pododermatitis lesions
e: Rabbit urine is alkaline and mineral-rich. Alkaline soaps cannot dissolve these mineral deposits. Acetic acid (pH 2–3) breaks down calcium and mineral buildup on caging and litter boxes before or in place of standard disinfection.

q: A rabbit's urine appears red-orange. What is the most appropriate next step to distinguish porphyrinuria from hematuria?
o: Renal ultrasound
Wood's lamp examination — porphyrins fluoresce pink/orange under UV while blood does not
Urine culture and sensitivity
Abdominal radiographs
e: Rabbit urine contains porphyrins that can cause red/orange/brown discoloration mimicking hematuria. A Wood's lamp rapidly differentiates porphyrinuria from true hematuria without invasive diagnostics.

q: What is the correct order for cleaning rabbit housing when both healthy rabbits and RHDV-quarantine animals are present in the shelter?
o: RHDV quarantine rabbits first to allow maximum drying time, then healthy adults, then kits
Healthy kits → healthy adults → unhealthy rabbits; RHDV quarantine animals are cleaned AFTER the healthy population, with separate supplies
All rabbits cleaned simultaneously with designated staff assigned to each group
Unhealthy rabbits first, then healthy, then kits
e: Clean from most vulnerable to most infectious: healthy kits → healthy adults → unhealthy. RHDV quarantine animals are cleaned last to prevent environmental contamination spreading to the healthy population.

q: What co-housing requirement applies to all group-housed rabbits per ASV 2026?
o: Intact adult rabbits can be co-housed if well-socialized and monitored closely
All group-housed rabbits must be spayed/neutered; co-housing intact adult rabbits risks serious fighting causing injury or death
Males and females of any reproductive status can share exercise space freely
Group housing is permitted only for same-sex bonded pairs adopted together
e: All rabbits in group housing must be spayed/neutered. Co-housing intact adult rabbits risks serious injury and death from fighting. Rabbits of opposite sex should be separated for a minimum of 2 weeks following sterilization.

q: A shelter rabbit is scheduled for spay surgery next week. What is the ideal perioperative housing arrangement?
o: Housed with other surgical patients of all species for mutual comfort
Quiet, low-stress housing separated from dogs, cats, and ferrets; rabbit surgeries scheduled on days when cat/dog surgeries are not occurring; bonded companions kept together
In the main rabbit ward with conspecifics
Darkened isolation unit without enrichment to minimize stimulation
e: Perioperative rabbit housing must be quiet and separated from predator species. Scheduling rabbit surgeries on non-dog/cat days minimizes shared-space stress. Bonded pairs are kept together to reduce perioperative stress.

q: Why does housing more rabbits not result in proportionally more adoptions, per ASV 2026 capacity planning?
o: Rabbits compete with each other for adopter attention, reducing individual placement rates
Doubling the population with the same adoption rate doubles average length of stay and care demands while potentially overwhelming adopters with choice
Shelters have legal limits on rabbit numbers unrelated to care capacity
More rabbits always require larger staff ratios that reduce overall productivity
e: With a fixed adoption rate (e.g., 10/month), doubling housed rabbits from 10 to 20 doubles ALOS from 1 to 2 months, doubles enrichment and care demands, and can paradoxically reduce adoptions by overwhelming adopters with choice.

q: What disinfectant properties are specifically required for RHDV disinfection in rabbit housing?
o: Disinfectants effective against enveloped viruses only (standard QAC) are sufficient

Disinfectants effective against non-enveloped viruses are required because RHDV is a non-enveloped calicivirus; options include accelerated hydrogen peroxide, potassium peroxymonosulfate, and 0.5% sodium hypochlorite
Any hospital-grade product is suitable regardless of viral spectrum
Bleach is specifically contraindicated in rabbit areas due to respiratory toxicity
e: RHDV is a non-enveloped calicivirus resistant to many disinfectants that work against enveloped viruses. Shelters must use agents with proven non-enveloped virus efficacy: accelerated hydrogen peroxide, potassium peroxymonosulfate, or 0.5% NaOCl.

q: What is the minimum enclosure width recommended when co-housing two rabbits, and why?
o: 1.5 m (5 ft), because rabbits naturally rest 2–5 body lengths apart
0.9 m (3 ft), equivalent to single rabbit minimum width
e: Co-housed rabbits naturally maintain a distance of 2–5 body lengths during rest. A minimum width of 1.5 m (4.9 ft) accommodates this natural spacing behavior and reduces stress-related conflict in paired housing.

q: A ferret is vaccinated against canine distemper at shelter intake. Twenty minutes later it becomes lethargic with vomiting and collapse. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Systemic CDV infection present at intake; antiviral therapy
Anaphylaxis to the CDV vaccine; diphenhydramine 2–4 mg/kg IM/IV and supportive care, with epinephrine for severe cases
Hypoglycemia from a missed meal; oral dextrose
Ear mite-induced vestibular crisis; aural ivermectin
e: Ferrets have a high prevalence of anaphylactic reactions to CDV and rabies vaccines, typically within 25 minutes of vaccination. Diphenhydramine 2–4 mg/kg IM/IV is first-line; epinephrine, dexamethasone, and oxygen support may be needed.

q: Canine distemper virus (CDV) is confirmed in a shelter ferret. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Isolate and treat with supportive care; prognosis is guarded but some ferrets recover
Humane euthanasia is recommended — CDV is 100% fatal in ferrets; separate all exposed animals and vaccinate all healthy unvaccinated ferrets
Transfer immediately to a specialty ferret hospital for antiviral therapy
Administer anti-canine distemper hyperimmune serum and monitor for 4 weeks
e: CDV is uniformly fatal in ferrets — 100% case fatality rate with no effective treatment. Euthanasia minimizes suffering and outbreak risk. All healthy unvaccinated shelter ferrets in contact should be immediately vaccinated.

q: A 2-year-old spayed female ferret in a shelter develops bilateral symmetrical alopecia starting at the tail base progressing rostrally, plus vulvar swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Dermatophytosis (ringworm)
Adrenocortical disease
Aleutian disease virus (ADV)
Normal seasonal weight fluctuation
e: Adrenocortical disease: bilateral symmetrical alopecia (tail-to-head progression) plus vulvar swelling in a spayed female is the classic presentation. This condition is strongly associated with early-age spay/neuter and is almost exclusively described in US ferret populations.

q: A guinea pig presents with severe pruritus, excoriations, and seizure-like scratching episodes. Skin scraping confirms a mite infestation. What is the causative mite and its zoonotic status?
o: Psoroptes cuniculi; not zoonotic
Trixacarus caviae; ZOONOTIC — can temporarily infect humans causing pruritic skin lesions
Demodex caviae; no zoonotic risk
Cheyletiella parasitovorax; high zoonotic risk requiring immediate isolation
e: Trixacarus caviae (sarcoptic mite of guinea pigs) causes severe pruritus that can mimic seizure activity. It is ZOONOTIC — can cause a temporary pruritic skin reaction in humans. Treatment: ivermectin 0.2–0.4 mg/kg SQ q10–14d × 3 doses.

q: Why is vitamin C supplementation critical for guinea pigs in shelter care?
o: Guinea pigs have a very high metabolic rate requiring vitamin C as an antioxidant cofactor
Guinea pigs cannot synthesize vitamin C endogenously and will develop scurvy without dietary supplementation
Vitamin C is required for normal cecotroph production
Guinea pigs excrete vitamin C unusually rapidly through alkaline urine
e: Guinea pigs lack L-gulonolactone oxidase and cannot synthesize vitamin C. Deficiency causes scurvy. Supplement via species-formulated guinea pig pellets and fresh vegetables (kale, bell peppers, oranges).

q: A shelter coordinator proposes using pine shavings as bedding for guinea pigs. The correct response is:
o: Pine shavings are the preferred substrate for guinea pigs
Pine and cedar shavings are contraindicated — aromatic hydrocarbons cause respiratory and skin disease; use paper-based substrates, recycled newspaper pellets, or hardwood shavings instead
Pine is acceptable; only cedar is contraindicated
Both are acceptable if changed at least once weekly
e: Pine and cedar shavings contain aromatic hydrocarbons causing respiratory irritation and health problems in guinea pigs and small rodents. Paper-based bedding (shredded paper, newspaper pellets) is recommended.

q: Which of the following shelter animal species can be an asymptomatic carrier of Bordetella bronchiseptica capable of infecting guinea pigs?
o: Only other guinea pigs
Rabbits, dogs, cats, and non-human primates — all can carry B. bronchiseptica asymptomatically
Only dogs and cats
Only wild birds and mice
e: B. bronchiseptica has a very broad host range. Rabbits, dogs, cats, and non-human primates can all be asymptomatic carriers that infect guinea pigs — even sharing the same airspace can be sufficient for transmission.

q: Which disinfectant is specifically contraindicated for use in reptile and amphibian enclosures?
o: Dilute bleach (1:32 dilution)
Quaternary ammonium compounds (QAC)
Phenolic compounds and glutaraldehyde
Accelerated hydrogen peroxide
e: Phenolic compounds and glutaraldehyde are specifically toxic to reptiles and amphibians and must never be used in their enclosures. Dilute bleach (1:32) and QAC are recommended disinfectants, followed by thorough rinsing.

q: A rat develops progressive respiratory noise, sneezing, and chronic bronchopneumonia. Doxycycline plus enrofloxacin reduces clinical signs but the rat relapses when antibiotics are discontinued. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Sendai virus — self-limiting infection resolving within 2 weeks
Mycoplasma pulmonis — the most common major respiratory pathogen in rats; infection is lifelong and cannot be eradicated, only managed with ongoing antibiotic therapy
Streptococcus pneumoniae — recurrence means the treatment course was too short
Bordetella bronchiseptica — completely eliminated with a full 4-week antibiotic course
e: M. pulmonis is an obligate intracellular bacterium — infection is lifelong and incurable. Doxycycline plus enrofloxacin controls clinical signs but does not eliminate infection. Recrudescence on cessation of antibiotics is the norm. Affected rats should be segregated.

q: What is 'wet tail' in hamsters, which age group is most affected, and what is the approximate mortality rate without treatment?
o: Bordetella bronchiseptica infection in adult hamsters; mortality 10%
Lawsonia intracellularis proliferative ileitis in young weanling hamsters (4–8 weeks); mortality approaches 90%
Rotavirus gastroenteritis in neonatal hamsters under 2 weeks; mortality 5%
Helicobacter-associated gastritis in adult hamsters; chronic low-grade disease with rare acute mortality
e: Wet tail is caused by Lawsonia intracellularis (obligate intracellular bacterium) and occurs in stressed weanling hamsters. Mortality approaches 90% without aggressive treatment: IV/SC fluids, antibiotics (metronidazole, tetracycline, enrofloxacin, TMS), and nutritional support.

q: Why is oral (enteral) penicillin contraindicated in rabbits, and what is the correct route for treating rabbit syphilis (Treponema)?
o: It is inactivated by gastric acid; give it with food instead
It disrupts the cecal microbiome causing fatal Clostridium overgrowth (enterotoxaemia); use injectable penicillin G instead
Rabbits are allergic to all penicillins; use oral amoxicillin
It is nephrotoxic orally; give it intravenously
e: Enteral penicillin disrupts the cecal flora and causes fatal Clostridium overgrowth (antibiotic-associated enterotoxaemia). Rabbit syphilis (Treponema paraluiscuniculi) is treated with INJECTABLE penicillin G in all exposed rabbits; oral penicillin must never be given.

q: A shelter rabbit with fleas needs treatment. Which product is specifically contraindicated in rabbits?
o: Imidacloprid
Selamectin
Fipronil
Lufenuron
e: Fipronil is contraindicated in rabbits (associated with toxicity and death). Imidacloprid, lufenuron and selamectin are generally safe (selamectin is metabolized faster than in cats, needing a different regimen). Dog/cat tick products, flea/tick collars and insecticide dips must also be avoided in rabbits.

q: Which set of properties correctly characterizes Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus (RHDV) for shelter management?
o: Enveloped togavirus, not reportable, killed by any hospital disinfectant
Non-enveloped calicivirus, REPORTABLE, requires non-enveloped-virus disinfectants (0.5% sodium hypochlorite or 1% formalin); neonates are resistant
Enveloped coronavirus, reportable, neonates most susceptible
Non-enveloped parvovirus, not reportable, only affects wild hares
e: RHDV is a non-enveloped calicivirus and a reportable disease affecting domestic/European rabbits over 2 months (neonates are resistant). Being non-enveloped it resists many disinfectants — use 0.5% sodium hypochlorite or 1% formalin. Absence of orifice bleeding does not rule it out.

q: A dwarf-breed shelter rabbit develops head tilt, nystagmus and hind-limb paresis. Which intracellular organism (a microsporidian fungus) is the most likely cause?
o: Pasteurella multocida
Encephalitozoon cuniculi
Treponema paraluiscuniculi
Eimeria stiedae
e: In dwarf breeds, vestibular disease (head tilt) is most often Encephalitozoon cuniculi — an intracellular microsporidian (fungus) with seroprevalence 7.5–84.7% that targets brain, kidney, lens and myocardium. In standard breeds, Pasteurella/otitis is the more likely cause. Serology does not correlate with severity; no treatment reliably clears it.

q: Which rodent-associated organism is the primary cause of rat-bite fever in humans?
o: Leptospira interrogans
Streptobacillus moniliformis
Mycoplasma pulmonis
Lawsonia intracellularis
e: Streptobacillus moniliformis is the primary cause of rat-bite fever. Wild and pet rats are asymptomatic carriers (nasopharynx, middle ear, respiratory tract; present in urine and blood). Transmission via bites, scratches, handling excreta, or contaminated food/water — handle with PPE and good hygiene.
